questions.subject: Maths
questions.series: Original Pure practice linked to AQA June 2022 Paper 1 methods
questions.prompt: The sequence uₙ=cos(nπ/2) is defined for positive integers n. Write the first eight terms, give its least positive period and calculate the sum of those eight terms. [4 marks]
markPoints: Evaluating n=1,2,3,4 gives 0,−1,0,1.
The next four terms repeat the same sequence: 0,−1,0,1.
The least positive period is 4, because shifting n by 4 leaves every term unchanged.
The sum of the first eight terms is twice (0−1+0+1)=0.
questions.modelAnswer: Evaluating n=1,2,3,4 gives 0,−1,0,1. The next four terms repeat the same sequence: 0,−1,0,1. The least positive period is 4, because shifting n by 4 leaves every term unchanged. The sum of the first eight terms is twice (0−1+0+1)=0.

questions.prompt: Starting from the graph y=log₂x, the graph is stretched vertically by factor 2 and translated upwards by 1. State the transformed equation, its domain and its x-intercept. [4 marks]
markPoints: The vertical stretch multiplies function values by 2.
Adding 1 translates the curve upwards, giving y=2log₂x+1.
The domain remains x>0.
At the x-intercept log₂x=−1/2, hence x=2^(−1/2)=1/√2.
questions.modelAnswer: The vertical stretch multiplies function values by 2. Adding 1 translates the curve upwards, giving y=2log₂x+1. The domain remains x>0. At the x-intercept log₂x=−1/2, hence x=2^(−1/2)=1/√2.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.series: Original Pure practice linked to AQA June 2022 Paper 1 methods
questions.prompt: A curve has equation y=x²−4x+3. Find the equation of the gradient graph y=f′(x), its intercepts with both axes, and describe when the original curve decreases. [4 marks]
markPoints: Differentiate to obtain f′(x)=2x−4.
The gradient graph is a straight line with y-intercept −4.
Its x-intercept is x=2, where the original quadratic has a stationary point.
Since 2x−4<0 for x<2, the original curve is decreasing on x<2.
questions.modelAnswer: Differentiate to obtain f′(x)=2x−4. The gradient graph is a straight line with y-intercept −4. Its x-intercept is x=2, where the original quadratic has a stationary point. Since 2x−4<0 for x<2, the original curve is decreasing on x<2.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.series: Original Pure practice linked to AQA June 2022 Paper 1 methods
questions.prompt: Find the tangent to y=(x²+3)³ at x=1. Show the chain-rule calculation and give your answer in the form y=mx+c. [4 marks]
markPoints: At x=1, the curve has y=(1+3)³=64.
By the chain rule, dy/dx=3(x²+3)²×2x=6x(x²+3)².
At x=1, the gradient is 6×16=96.
The tangent equation y−64=96(x−1) becomes y=96x−32.
questions.modelAnswer: At x=1, the curve has y=(1+3)³=64. By the chain rule, dy/dx=3(x²+3)²×2x=6x(x²+3)². At x=1, the gradient is 6×16=96. The tangent equation y−64=96(x−1) becomes y=96x−32.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.series: Original Pure practice linked to AQA June 2022 Paper 1 methods
questions.prompt: Find the first three non-zero terms of (1−2x)^(-1/2), state the validity interval and use them to estimate the value at x=0.1. [5 marks]
markPoints: Use (1+u)ⁿ=1+nu+[n(n−1)/2]u²+⋯ with n=−1/2 and u=−2x.
The constant and linear terms are 1+x.
The quadratic term is [(−1/2)(−3/2)/2]×4x²=(3/2)x².
questions.modelAnswer: Use (1+u)ⁿ=1+nu+[n(n−1)/2]u²+⋯ with n=−1/2 and u=−2x. The constant and linear terms are 1+x. The quadratic term is [(−1/2)(−3/2)/2]×4x²=(3/2)x². Thus (1−2x)^(-1/2)≈1+x+(3/2)x² for |x|<1/2. At x=0.1 this gives 1+0.1+0.015=1.115.

questions.prompt: For 0<x<2π, find all vertical asymptotes and zeroes of y=cot(x−π/4), and explain the graph transformation from y=cot x. [5 marks]
markPoints: Replacing x by x−π/4 translates the cotangent graph right by π/4.
Cotangent has asymptotes when its argument is an integer multiple of π.
Hence the asymptotes in 0<x<2π are x=π/4 and x=5π/4.
Zeroes occur when x−π/4=π/2+kπ, giving x=3π/4 and x=7π/4.
The curve decreases between adjacent vertical asymptotes because the derivative of cot is −csc².
questions.modelAnswer: Replacing x by x−π/4 translates the cotangent graph right by π/4. Cotangent has asymptotes when its argument is an integer multiple of π. Hence the asymptotes in 0<x<2π are x=π/4 and x=5π/4. Zeroes occur when x−π/4=π/2+kπ, giving x=3π/4 and x=7π/4. The curve decreases between adjacent vertical asymptotes because the derivative of cot is −csc².

questions.series: Original Pure practice linked to AQA June 2022 Paper 1 methods
questions.prompt: A circle has centre (2,−1) and radius 5. Verify that (5,3) lies on it and find the tangent line at that point. [5 marks]
markPoints: The displacement from the centre to (5,3) is (3,4), whose length is √(3²+4²)=5.
Therefore the point is on the circle.
The radius gradient is 4/3.
The tangent is perpendicular, so its gradient is −3/4.
The tangent equation is y−3=−(3/4)(x−5).
questions.modelAnswer: The displacement from the centre to (5,3) is (3,4), whose length is √(3²+4²)=5. Therefore the point is on the circle. The radius gradient is 4/3. The tangent is perpendicular, so its gradient is −3/4. The tangent equation is y−3=−(3/4)(x−5).

questions.subject: Maths
questions.series: Original Pure practice linked to AQA June 2022 Paper 1 methods
questions.prompt: An arithmetic sequence begins 8,11,14,... Find a formula for its nth term and its sum Sₙ. Determine the first n for which uₙ≥80 and calculate Sₙ at that point. [5 marks]
markPoints: First term a=8 and common difference d=3.
To have uₙ≥80 requires 3n+5≥80, so n≥25.
questions.modelAnswer: First term a=8 and common difference d=3. uₙ=8+3(n−1)=3n+5. Sₙ=n[2×8+(n−1)3]/2=n(3n+13)/2. To have uₙ≥80 requires 3n+5≥80, so n≥25. At n=25 the sum is 25(3×25+13)/2=1100.

questions.series: Original Pure practice linked to AQA June 2022 Paper 1 methods
questions.prompt: Use two Newton–Raphson iterations to approximate the positive root of x²−5=0 from x₀=2. Give the iterates and the root to three decimal places. [4 marks]
markPoints: For f(x)=x²−5, the derivative is f′(x)=2x.
The iteration is xₙ₊₁=xₙ−(xₙ²−5)/(2xₙ)=(xₙ+5/xₙ)/2.
Starting from x₀=2 gives x₁=(2+5/2)/2=2.25.
Then x₂=(2.25+5/2.25)/2=2.236111...; hence the root is approximately 2.236.
questions.modelAnswer: For f(x)=x²−5, the derivative is f′(x)=2x. The iteration is xₙ₊₁=xₙ−(xₙ²−5)/(2xₙ)=(xₙ+5/xₙ)/2. Starting from x₀=2 gives x₁=(2+5/2)/2=2.25. Then x₂=(2.25+5/2.25)/2=2.236111...; hence the root is approximately 2.236.

questions.prompt: Let P(x)=x³−4x²+4x. Show that x−2 is a factor, factorise P(x) fully and explain which x-intercepts the cubic crosses or touches. [5 marks]
markPoints: Factor theorem: P(2)=8−16+8=0, so x−2 is a factor.
Factor out x to obtain P(x)=x(x²−4x+4).
Hence P(x)=x(x−2)².
The simple root x=0 crosses the x-axis.
The double root x=2 touches, rather than crosses, the x-axis.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.series: Original Pure practice linked to AQA June 2022 Paper 1 methods
questions.prompt: A geometric sequence has first term 5 and common ratio sin(π/6). Find the exact sum to infinity and the smallest n for which the partial sum Sₙ exceeds 9.8. [5 marks]
markPoints: Since sin(π/6)=1/2, the common ratio is r=1/2 with |r|<1.
The sum to infinity is S∞=5/(1−1/2)=10.
The nth partial sum is Sₙ=10(1−2^(−n)).
Sₙ>9.8 is equivalent to 2^(−n)<0.02=1/50.
Thus 2ⁿ>50, so the smallest positive integer n is 6.
questions.modelAnswer: Since sin(π/6)=1/2, the common ratio is r=1/2 with |r|<1. The sum to infinity is S∞=5/(1−1/2)=10. The nth partial sum is Sₙ=10(1−2^(−n)). Sₙ>9.8 is equivalent to 2^(−n)<0.02=1/50. Thus 2ⁿ>50, so the smallest positive integer n is 6.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.series: Original Pure practice linked to AQA June 2022 Paper 1 methods
questions.prompt: The curve x²+xy+y²=12 passes through (2,2). Find dy/dx, the tangent at (2,2), and the coordinates where the curve has a horizontal tangent. [6 marks]
markPoints: Implicit differentiation gives 2x+y+x(dy/dx)+2y(dy/dx)=0.
Rearranging: dy/dx=−(2x+y)/(x+2y).
At (2,2) the gradient is −6/6=−1, so the tangent is y−2=−(x−2), or x+y=4.
For horizontal tangents dy/dx=0, so 2x+y=0, provided x+2y≠0.
Substitute y=−2x into the curve to give x²−2x²+4x²=12, hence 3x²=12 and x=±2.
The two horizontal-tangent points are (2,−4) and (−2,4); both have nonzero denominator.
questions.modelAnswer: Implicit differentiation gives 2x+y+x(dy/dx)+2y(dy/dx)=0. Rearranging: dy/dx=−(2x+y)/(x+2y). At (2,2) the gradient is −6/6=−1, so the tangent is y−2=−(x−2), or x+y=4. For horizontal tangents dy/dx=0, so 2x+y=0, provided x+2y≠0. Substitute y=−2x into the curve to give x²−2x²+4x²=12, hence 3x²=12 and x=±2. The two horizontal-tangent points are (2,−4) and (−2,4); both have nonzero denominator.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.series: Original Pure practice linked to AQA June 2022 Paper 1 methods
questions.prompt: Evaluate exactly the definite integral ∫₁ᵉ x ln x dx, using integration by parts. [5 marks]
markPoints: Choose u=ln x and dv=x dx, so du=dx/x and v=x²/2.
By integration by parts, ∫x ln x dx=(x²/2)ln x−(1/2)∫x dx.
An antiderivative is (x²/2)ln x−x²/4.
At x=e this equals e²/2−e²/4=e²/4.
At x=1 it equals −1/4, so the definite integral is (e²+1)/4.
questions.modelAnswer: Choose u=ln x and dv=x dx, so du=dx/x and v=x²/2. By integration by parts, ∫x ln x dx=(x²/2)ln x−(1/2)∫x dx. An antiderivative is (x²/2)ln x−x²/4. At x=e this equals e²/2−e²/4=e²/4. At x=1 it equals −1/4, so the definite integral is (e²+1)/4.

questions.prompt: For 0<x<π, differentiate y=cosec x from y=1/sin x. Hence evaluate ∫cos x/sin²x dx. [4 marks]
markPoints: Write y=(sin x)^(−1).
The chain rule gives dy/dx=−(sin x)^(−2)cos x.
This is −cos x/sin²x=−cosec x cot x.
Therefore ∫cos x/sin²x dx=−cosec x+C.
